parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to model a two time series as random walks with correlated error terms. However, the sampler doesn't complete its warmup. Any help would be appreciated. Thanks.

N is the number of data points and M is the number of series (in this case it is two). 
data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=1> M;
vector[M] y[N];

}
parameters { 
vector[M] mu;
real<lower=0> sigma[2];
real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho;

}
transformed parameters {
cov_matrix[2] Sigma;


Sigma[1,2] <- rho* sigma[1] * sigma[2];
Sigma[2,1] <- Sigma[1,2];
Sigma[1,1] <- square(sigma[1]);
Sigma[2,2] <- square(sigma[2]);

}


model{

for(n in 2:N){
y[n]~multi_normal(y[n-1],Sigma);

}

}

parts:
Good catch.

The problem with the mu parameter with no distribution
specified is that Stan treats it as uniform on (-infinity, infinity),
which leads to an improper posterior. Stan requires proper
posteriors to sample. One way to guarantee this is with proper
priors, but Stan can handle improper priors as long as the posterior
is proper. There's a chapter discussing why such posteriors are
problematic in the manual.

- Bob

> Hi again. I'm running the code below (same data) but its taking over 24 hours to complete... I'd like to do this with more than 2 time series as well. Is the code misspecified or inefficiently writen?

> matrix[K,K] SigmaV;
> matrix[K,K] SigmaW;
> cov_matrix[2] Sigmavprior;

> SigmaV <- diag_matrix(tauV) * OmegaV * diag_matrix(tauV);
>
> SigmaW <- diag_matrix(tauW) * OmegaW * diag_matrix(tauW);

There are more efficient scaling operations. diag_pre_multiply()
and diag_post_multiply() in Stan 2.2. In Stan 2.3 (out any
minute, really), there will also be a direct quadratic form that
will do this all at once.

>
>
> Sigmavprior[1,1] <- 100;
> Sigmavprior[2,2]<- 100;
> Sigmavprior[1,2] <- 0;
> Sigmavprior[2,1] <- 0;
>
> }

If you have anything constant like Sigmavprior, it's much
more efficient to define it as transformed data. All variables
should basically be declared in the earliest block that's feasible.

Also, no point making a diagonal covariance matrix. You can just
sample the components independently with a vectorized univariate
normal, replacing
> theta[1]~multi_normal(y[1], Sigmavprior);

with

theta[1] ~ multi_normal(y[1],100);

Now having said all this, you probably want to work directly
with Cholesky factors. You can do this one of two ways. Either
declare the Cholesky factors as variables (more efficient), or
Cholesky factorize a covariance matrix in the model itself and reuse
it with multi_normal_cholesky(). Alas, the Cholesky factor for
covariance matrix type is broken due to a misspelled error check in
2.2 (Ben --- this is why we try to be thorough in our signature
tests --- this one obviously didn't have enough testing); that's fixed
in 2.3 and there's also a Cholesky factor for correlation matrices type
and some explicit advice on how to use it in the manual.

> model{
> //prior
> theta[1]~multi_normal(y[1], Sigmavprior);
> //likelihood
> for(n in 2:N){
> theta[n]~multi_normal(theta[n-1],SigmaW);
> y[n]~multi_normal(theta[n],SigmaV);
>
> }
>

The implicit prior on covariances is improper, which can slow
down sampling --- are you seeing big excursions?

I like the first line written the other way around as
the equivalent

y[1] ~ multi_normal(theta[1], Sigmavprior);

to make it clear it's really part of the likelihood and to
make it clear you don't really have a prior here for theta[1].
Then you can add

theta[1] ~ normal(0,100);

if you want, but that prior's probably so weak as to have almost
no effect if your data are on a standardized scale.

- Bob

I've successfully got my model to work! Very exciting.. Now I'd like to forecast my time series. I can't find any documentation to do this (no results come up when searching for "forecasting" in stan reference). Can someone suggest a place to look?

ode1=
  "data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=1> K;
vector[K] y[N];

int<lower=1>  S;
  int<lower=1>  dum[N]; // monthly dummies

}
parameters { 
corr_matrix[K] OmegaV;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauV;
corr_matrix[K] OmegaW;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauW;
vector[K] theta[N];

vector[K]  alpha[S];
vector[K] mu[N];
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_mu;



}
transformed parameters{
matrix[K,K] L_betaV;
matrix[K,K] L_betaW;

L_betaV <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaV);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaV[k1,k2] <- tauV[k1] * L_betaV[k1,k2];

L_betaW <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaW);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaW[k1,k2] <- tauW[k1] * L_betaW[k1,k2];


}



model{
//prior
mu[1] ~ normal(0, 1.0e+5 );
theta[1]~normal(y[1], 100);
y[1]~multi_normal_cholesky(theta[1], L_betaV);

//likelihood
for(n in 2:N){

mu[n]~normal(mu[n-1], sigma_mu);
theta[n]~multi_normal_cholesky(mu[n]+theta[n-1],L_betaW);
y[n]~multi_normal_cholesky(alpha[ dum[n] ]  + theta[n],L_betaV);

}

}


"

We talk about forecasting as "predictive inference". We should
add the "forecasting" terminology to aid in search. We talk about it in the
description of Bayesian inference in the intro and later on, and in a bunch of
examples, such as Gaussian processes and naive Bayes. I added a note
to the next manual issue to add an example for regression and time series:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/668#issuecomment-47424210

There are two ways to do this.

Both involve adding new data variables for the number of items to
predict/forecast and any inputs necessary to do that prediction.
Then you can either:

1. Define new parameters for the predictions and give these parameters
predictions just like in the original model. This only works for continous
predictions.

2. Define new generated quantity variables for the predictions and
define them using random number generators in the generated quantities block.
This will work for discrete or continous predictions.

- Bob

parts:
This code doesn't work for a large number of variables (time series). When I run the code for two time series, it takes a long time to simulate (about an hour) and the results adequate. When I want to include something like 10 variables (in this case have 10 time series in my SUR), it takes a minute and gives values of all parameters around zero. 

Why does including more variables (in this case having a larger K) give inadequate results? (My thought is that the parameter space is too big / constrained and its not sampling properly.. Just a guess)

Thanks Again

Below is code: 

code1=
  "data {
int<lower=0> N1;
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> N2;
int<lower=1> K;
vector[K] y1[N1];

int<lower=1>  S;
int<lower=1>  dum[N]; // monthly dummies

}
parameters { 
corr_matrix[K] OmegaV;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauV;
corr_matrix[K] OmegaW;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauW;
vector[K] theta[N];
vector[K]  alpha[S];
vector[K] mu[N];
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_mu;
vector[K] y2[N2];

}
transformed parameters{
matrix[K,K] L_betaV;
matrix[K,K] L_betaW;

L_betaV <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaV);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaV[k1,k2] <- tauV[k1] * L_betaV[k1,k2];

L_betaW <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaW);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaW[k1,k2] <- tauW[k1] * L_betaW[k1,k2];

vector[K] y[N];

//likelihood

On Sat, Jun 28, 2014 at 1:44 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
We talk about forecasting as "predictive inference".  We should
add the "forecasting" terminology to aid in search.  We talk about it in the
description of Bayesian inference in the intro and later on, and in a bunch of
examples, such as Gaussian processes and naive Bayes.  I added a note
to the next manual issue to add an example for regression and time series:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/668#issuecomment-47424210

There are two ways to do this.

Both involve adding new data variables for the number of items to
predict/forecast and any inputs necessary to do that prediction.
Then you can either:

1.  Define new parameters for the predictions and give these parameters
predictions just like in the original model.  This only works for continous
predictions.

2.  Define new generated quantity variables for the predictions and
define them using random number generators in the generated quantities block.
This will work for discrete or continous predictions.

- Bob

Do you get warnings printed out as you go about failures
in the covariance matrix tests?

I'm hoping the problem is that our covariance matrix and
correlation matrix consistency checks are too stringent and
causing unnecessary failures. That's been the case before.

The underlying problem with more variables is that floating
point arithmetic just isn't that precise, and when you have
lots of operations (as in Cholesky factor multiplication
and solvers converting the constrained/unconstrained), the
results vary from what you'd get from infinite-precision
arithmetic in that we can lose symmetry or positive definiteness.

Another problem is if estimates get pushed up against boundaries
(here correlation = 1 or -1, sd = 0 or +infinity). This is
also very unstable arithmetically.

You might want to try again with Stan 2.4 --- we tried to clean
some of these things up, but we probably still have a ways to go.

- Bob

On Thu, Jul 24, 2014 at 12:49 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
Do you get warnings printed out as you go about failures
in the covariance matrix tests?

I'm hoping the problem is that our covariance matrix and
correlation matrix consistency checks are too stringent and
causing unnecessary failures.  That's been the case before.

The underlying problem with more variables is that floating
point arithmetic just isn't that precise, and when you have
lots of operations (as in Cholesky factor multiplication
and solvers converting the constrained/unconstrained), the
results vary from what you'd get from infinite-precision
arithmetic in that we can lose symmetry or positive definiteness.

Another problem is if estimates get pushed up against boundaries
(here correlation = 1 or -1, sd = 0 or +infinity).  This is
also very unstable arithmetically.

You might want to try again with Stan 2.4 --- we tried to clean
some of these things up, but we probably still have a ways to go.

- Bob
